To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) internalization and body image were related to one another across time; (2) body image and depressive affect were reciprocally and simultaneously related; (3) depressive affect and ED symptoms were reciprocally related; and (4) internalization was not related to either depressive affect or ED symptoms.

(a) internalization of the media ideal and body dissatisfaction were related reciproc ally and temporally; (b) internalization of thin ideals, body dissatisfaction, and depressive affect were related simultaneously; and (c), depressive affect and disor dered eating were related recip rocally and temporally.

1) Internalization and body image are reciprocally related over time, 2) Internalization, body image, and depressive affect are reciprocally and contemporaneously related to one another, and 3) Disordered eating and depressive affect are contemporaneously but not reciprocally related to one another.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sociocultural factors that influence the development and maintenance of eating disorders.
the development of eating pathology and the role of social factors in that development.
the role that sociocultural factors play in the development of disor- dered eating and the possible mechanisms through which these factors influence the development of eating disor- ders.

sociocultural factors, such as internalization of the ideal and body image, are related to disordered eating, but not in the direction that has typically been hypothesized.
sociocultural factors are not the sole determiners of the development of disor dered eating.
the sociocultural model of disordered eating is not supported, but that it is not rejected, either.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sociocultural variables are important in the development of disor dered eating, yet the causal pathways are complex and reciprocal.
the results support a socioculturally informed model of the development of eating problems in college women.
the thin ideal and body dissatisfaction are interrelated and that body dissatisfaction is related to depressive affect, but only when considered in the context of disordered eating.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sociocultural risk factors are related reciprocally to one another and to disordered eating, and that disordered eating is related reciprocally with depressive affect.
the sociocultural model is not the only model that can be used to understand the development of body image and disordered eating.
